newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Savings bank offers hope for CIC privatisation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Savings bank offers hope for CIC privatisation.

text.p: The French government appears to have little room for manoeuvre to privatise banking group CIC after the cancellation on Thursday of a sell-off tender which drew only two suitors, one of which was a non-starter.

One possibility which could get it out of the bind, however, would be a re-run of the privatisation tender next year with the possibility of attracting an offer from the Caisses d'Epargne, financial analysts say.

That would bring another bidder into the competition along with BNP and Societe Generale if they decided to resubmit bids, which would increase the pressure to meet government demands and could also push the price higher.

The decision to break off the privatisation of the regional bank grouping was announced by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on the grounds of public and staff objections and the fact that there was only one eligible offer, from BNP.

Societe Generale's bid was rejected by the privatisation commission for failing to meet the terms set by the government, the most crucial one being that any buyer should preserve CIC as a grouping of 11 regional banks.

Analysts believe the government's insistence that the buyer preserve CIC's regional integrity and other conditions imposed on the would-be buyer could only result in a limited number of suitors, and a limited offer price.

If the government sticks to those conditions, which it has repeatedly said are essential, one possible way out would be an offer from the Caisses d'Epargne, which would be in the running if it gave up its status as a savings bank group, they said.
The Caisses had been tipped as a serious contender but said in early October it had decided not to enter the race "despite the complementarities between the Caisses d'Epargne and the CIC.

Press reports at the time said there was resistance within the Caisse d'Epargne from the state-owned bank, the Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC), which has more than a third of the voting rights on the board. That would be one obstacle for the government to contend with.
Another obstacle has been its legal status as a savings bank group rather than a private corporation.

The Association of French banks, representing commercial banks, sent a warning shot across the bows of the Caisses in October on the grounds that a privatisation could possibly be open to legal challenge if it went to a group which was not a private corporation.
But Arthuis said recently the Caisses and the government were looking into the question of changing its status.

"I think the Caisses d'Epargne will probably change status and they would then be able to put themselves in the running, possibly next May or June," said one French bank analyst, who asked not to be identified.
Neither BNP not Societe Generale would say on Thursday if they would be ready to make a new offer.
Arthuis said that even if the government had abondoned the privatisation tender it was determined to sell the group off.
Selling CIC is seen as crucial to one of the other large privatisations planned by the government -- the sale of CIC's parent Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN).
Arthuis said on Thursday he was determined to go ahead with that privatisation as well but that he did not favour doing so before selling CIC.
